questions.prompt: When a warning appears during setup, the pilot says, “Just launch now. We'll figure it out in the air.” Which hazardous attitude most directly fits that statement?

choices.A: Invulnerability.
choices.B: Resignation.
choices.C: Impulsivity.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: The pilot is acting immediately without taking time to assess the warning.
Why A is incorrect: Invulnerability centers on a belief that an adverse event will not happen to oneself. The quoted behavior emphasizes acting without thinking.
Why B is incorrect: Resignation is the belief that one's actions cannot change the outcome.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A notice is active from 0545Z through 0715Z on a day when local clocks are turned back. The planned pass is logged directly in UTC, from 0640Z to 0650Z. The site is inside the lateral and vertical limits. What does the time information establish?

choices.A: The restriction does not apply because the notice uses Z instead of a local zone abbreviation.
choices.B: Only the first half of the pass is restricted because local time is repeated.
choices.C: The entire planned pass falls in the restriction window.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Both UTC times for the planned pass fall within the stated UTC interval. No local clock conversion is needed.
Why A is incorrect: Z means UTC and is a valid reference for the notice and the flight plan.
Why B is incorrect: The local change does not split or shorten the UTC interval.
Reference: FAA, Temporary Flight Restrictions — https://tfr.faa.gov/tfr3/
Reference: FAA AIM, §5-1-3, Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) System — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap5_section_1.html

questions.prompt: Midway through a structure inspection, the camera automatically changes zoom. On screen the wall suddenly looks farther away, but the observer reports that the aircraft has not moved. What should the pilot do?

choices.A: Fly toward the wall until it fills the same amount of the screen as before.
choices.B: Assume the drone has moved away because the wall appears smaller.
choices.C: Keep the verified standoff and use direct position cues to reassess distance before making a correction.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: A focal-length change alters the image scale without necessarily changing aircraft position. Use reliable position cues before adjusting separation.
Why A is incorrect: Restoring image size by flying closer could reduce the real standoff.
Why B is incorrect: A smaller image alone does not establish increased separation.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: Recovery Site Willow is currently occupied although quicker than Maple; Maple is clear and requires 73 seconds to reach and finish landing; Cedar is clear but requires 85 seconds. The reserve threshold occurs at 80 seconds.

The crew can maintain safe flight for at most 80 seconds before reaching the required energy reserve. The written scenario data provide the total time to complete landing at three recovery sites under current conditions. Which site is clear and can be reached and landed at before that limit?

choices.A: Site Willow only.
choices.B: Site Maple only.
choices.C: Site Cedar only.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Maple is clear, and the total landing time of 73 seconds leaves seven seconds before the stated limit.
Why A is incorrect: Willow is faster but is currently occupied, so it does not meet the stated conditions.
Why C is incorrect: Cedar is clear, but reaching the site and completing landing together take 85 seconds.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 11, Aircraft Performance — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: A steady illuminated red stop bar spans the taxiway at the holding position, under airport low-visibility procedures.

The written scenario data describe a view from a taxiway under local low-visibility procedures. The described lights are steady. What should an aircraft pilot do at the lighted line?

choices.A: Cross immediately if the runway looks clear.
choices.B: Stop and do not cross the illuminated bar.
choices.C: Continue because the bar marks the far end of the runway.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: An illuminated red stop bar indicates a stop. It is not crossed while illuminated.
Why A is incorrect: An apparently clear runway does not override a stop bar.
Why C is incorrect: The bar is across the taxiway at the holding position, rather than at the far runway end.
Reference: FAA AIM, §2-1-10, Airport and Taxiway Lights — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap2_section_1.html
Reference: FAA AIM, §4-3, Airport Operations — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_3.html

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: The surface observation contains the remark WSHFT 1732 FROPA; the observation itself is timestamped 1753Z.

The crew wants the reported time of the wind shift for its weather log. What time should it enter?
questions.explanation:
Why B works: WSHFT 1732 is the time of the reported wind shift. The FROPA remark associates it with frontal passage.
Why A is incorrect: 180 begins the wind direction group. It does not give an event time.
Why C is incorrect: 1753Z is the time of the observation itself.
Reference: FAA-H-8083-28B, Aviation Weather Handbook — https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook
Reference: NOAA Aviation Weather Center, PIREP and METAR coding information — https://aviationweather.gov/help/data/

questions.prompt: A Category 2 aircraft has an affected part that must be replaced to eliminate a safety defect. The operator has the manufacturer's corrective bulletin, but the aircraft still has the affected part installed. Can the operator rely on Category 2 eligibility for a flight over people now?

choices.A: No. The aircraft must actually meet the eligibility requirements before the flight.
choices.B: Yes. The original Category 2 label alone settles eligibility.
choices.C: Yes. Having the corrective bulletin on file counts as completing the correction.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Category 2 eligibility requires the aircraft to meet the design and safety-defect requirements, in addition to the declaration and label requirements.
Why B is incorrect: A label does not demonstrate correction of a known defect.
Why C is incorrect: Receiving a bulletin does not change the aircraft's physical condition.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.115 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.115
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.120 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.120
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.160 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.160

questions.prompt: The pilot says to hold at the north pad. A crew member reads back “hold at the south pad.” The crew has not started moving. What should the pilot do?

choices.A: Correct the location and obtain an accurate readback before relying on the instruction.
choices.B: Accept the response because the crew member repeated the word hold.
choices.C: Wait until the crew reaches a pad to see which one it chose.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: A readback exposes the mismatch. Correcting and confirming the location keeps both people working from the same instruction.
Why B is incorrect: The action was understood but the location was not.
Why C is incorrect: Waiting for movement sacrifices the opportunity to correct the error before it matters.
Reference: FAA AIM, §4-2, Radio Communications Phraseology and Techniques — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_2.html
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: The crew uses a hanging banner as an apparent reference while maintaining separation from a wall. Gusts cause the banner to move toward and away from the wall. A fixed corner of the wall is visible from a safer viewing position. How should the crew revise the maneuver?

choices.A: Move closer whenever the banner moves away so the distance to it stays constant.
choices.B: Keep using the banner because it makes wind easier to see.
choices.C: Pause close work, establish separation using fixed references, and resume only with a reliable standoff.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: A moving reference cannot reliably indicate separation from the wall. Stable references and a checked standoff improve the basis for the maneuver.
Why A is incorrect: Following the moving banner could reduce real clearance from the wall.
Why B is incorrect: The banner can show wind without being a dependable distance reference.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: During a job the pilot develops a sudden condition that interferes with safe control. A current, certificated remote pilot is available and ready to take command under a safe handoff plan. What should the impaired pilot do?

choices.A: Stop performing affected flight duties and use the safe transfer or recovery plan.
choices.B: Keep manipulating the controls under supervision, because supervision overrides the fitness requirement.
choices.C: Continue as remote PIC because the aircraft has already taken off.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The fitness rule applies to the operational duties when a condition interferes with safe operation. A safe transfer or recovery addresses the problem.
Why B is incorrect: Direct supervision does not cure a condition that prevents safe operation.
Why C is incorrect: Taking off does not make the pilot exempt from the continuing fitness requirement.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.17 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.17
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.12 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.12

questions.prompt: A standard Remote ID aircraft's only accepted declaration covering its serial number has been rescinded. The operator asserts a separately issued FAA design approval as the basis for the standard pathway. What should be verified before relying on that assertion?

choices.A: Only that the pilot's certificate is current.
choices.B: Only that the aircraft's printed label was applied before the rescission.
choices.C: That the applicable Part 21 design or production approval actually covers this aircraft and that it meets the relevant Part 89 Subpart F requirements.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 89.110(b)(1) recognizes an applicable design or production approval as an alternative to listing on an accepted declaration when the Subpart F requirements are met.
Why A is incorrect: Pilot currency cannot establish aircraft design or production compliance.
Why B is incorrect: An old label does not establish the alternative approval.
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.110 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.110
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.540 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.540

questions.prompt: An airport announcement says one runway has reopened. A separate current area notice still restricts drone flight over part of the planned route. Which information determines whether the route may enter that area?

choices.A: The reopening announcement alone, because it is the more recent airport message.
choices.B: The pilot's estimate of whether the reopened runway is far enough away.
choices.C: The applicable current area restriction and any stated exception or authorization.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Reopening a runway does not cancel a separate restriction covering a drone route. Check the governing notice.
Why A is incorrect: The airport message describes runway availability rather than permission under the separate notice.
Why B is incorrect: Distance from the runway does not resolve the published area's boundaries or conditions.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.47 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.47
Reference: FAA AIM, §5-1-3, Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) System — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap5_section_1.html
Reference: FAA AIM, §§4-1-3 and 4-1-9, Flight Service and traffic advisories — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_1.html

questions.prompt: A standard Remote ID prototype transmits one complete position and identity message every two seconds. The contents are otherwise correct. Does this schedule meet the required minimum message rate?

choices.A: No. It sends 0.5 messages per second, below the minimum of one per second.
choices.B: Yes. One complete message every two seconds meets the minimum.
choices.C: Yes. The rate requirement applies only to a broadcast module, never to a standard Remote ID aircraft.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The standard design has a minimum of one message per second. One every two seconds is half that rate.
Why B is incorrect: A complete set of message elements must also be transmitted at the required rate.
Why C is incorrect: The standard aircraft requirements explicitly include a minimum rate.
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.310 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.310

questions.prompt: A metal screen has blocked the verified link path to the emergency landing area. An alternate landing area is clear and the planner has entered it in the app, but nobody has confirmed that the link and lost-link settings support that recovery. What remains before launch?

choices.A: Keep the former emergency area because the primary survey path still has good link coverage.
choices.B: Accept the alternate because the app accepted its coordinates.
choices.C: Verify the alternate with the current site and aircraft configuration, including the command link and applicable lost-link behavior.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: A mapped point does not establish that the aircraft can reach or recover there under the actual contingency. Verify the relevant behavior in the changed setup.
Why A is incorrect: A usable normal route does not restore the former recovery path.
Why B is incorrect: Coordinate acceptance is different from a verified contingency.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.49 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.49
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: Candidate Birch last drank ten hours before the flight and has alcohol concentration below 0.04. Each other candidate fails at least one of those two independently required screening conditions.

The written scenario data provide verified values at the planned flight time. Assume none of the candidates is under the influence, none has another disqualifying condition, and all are otherwise qualified. Which candidate meets both the minimum time since drinking and the alcohol concentration limit?

choices.A: Candidate Birch only.
choices.B: Candidate Cedar only.
choices.C: Candidate Aspen only.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Birch last drank ten hours ago and is below 0.04. Both displayed values meet the applicable limits.
Why B is incorrect: Cedar's eleven hours meet the time test, but an alcohol concentration of exactly 0.040 is disqualifying.
Why C is incorrect: Aspen's value is below 0.04, but only seven hours have elapsed.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.27 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.27
Reference: 14 CFR § 91.17 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/section-91.17

questions.prompt: A drone has prior authorization for a Class D segment through 200 feet AGL. Over rising terrain, the proposed route at 180 feet AGL also enters an overlying Class B shelf that begins at 150 feet AGL along that part of the route. The approval expressly covers only Class D. Which change is needed?

choices.A: Stay below the Class B floor there or obtain authorization that covers the Class B entry.
choices.B: Continue at 180 feet because it is below the numerical cap of the Class D authorization.
choices.C: Contact a different advisory frequency without changing the route or approval.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The altitude cap is not permission to enter a separate Class B volume that the authorization does not cover.
Why B is incorrect: The 200-foot cap applies only to the scope of the existing authorization.
Why C is incorrect: Monitoring or using an advisory frequency does not authorize the Class B entry.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.41 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.41
Reference: FAA AIM, §3-2, Controlled Airspace — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap3_section_2.html
Reference: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations — https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/part_107_airspace_authorizations

questions.prompt: A company is creating a training record for a newly certificated Part 107 remote pilot. Which rating belongs in the record for this FAA certificate?

choices.A: Airplane single-engine land rating.
choices.B: Instrument helicopter rating.
choices.C: Small UAS rating.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: The Part 107 credential is a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating.
Why A is incorrect: An airplane category and class rating belongs to a different type of pilot certification.
Why B is incorrect: An instrument helicopter rating is not the Part 107 small UAS rating.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.12 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.12
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.63 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.63

questions.prompt: A scripted demonstration allows a ground technician to monitor the aircraft but locks the remote PIC out of directing it until the program finishes. The lockout can be removed before launch. What should the remote PIC do?

choices.A: Remove the lockout and verify an effective way to direct the aircraft to ensure compliance.
choices.B: Leave the lockout in place if the project manager approves the demonstration.
choices.C: Accept the lockout because a programmed flight plan transfers the remote PIC's authority to the software.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The remote PIC must be able to direct the aircraft to ensure compliance. The stated lockout prevents that intervention.
Why B is incorrect: Project approval does not fix the loss of intervention ability.
Why C is incorrect: Automation does not take over the remote PIC's legal duty or ability to direct the operation.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.19 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.19
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.49 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.49

questions.prompt: A town is near an airport with an active Class E surface area designated for the airport. The planned drone flight is entirely outside that area's lateral limits at 100 feet AGL, and no other relevant controlled airspace or restriction applies. Is prior ATC authorization required solely because of that surface designation?

choices.A: Yes. Any flight within the town must use the airport surface authorization.
choices.B: No. The operation remains outside the lateral boundaries of that airport surface area.
choices.C: Yes. Any Class E designation shown anywhere in the same chart panel requires authorization.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Section 107.41 addresses operation within the lateral boundaries of the Class E surface area designated for an airport.
Why A is incorrect: Municipal boundaries are not the boundaries in the rule.
Why C is incorrect: Other charted designations do not automatically apply to this flight.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.41 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.41
Reference: FAA AIM, §3-2, Controlled Airspace — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap3_section_2.html

questions.prompt: A proposed Part 107 route crosses directly above a small cloud patch. The crew proposes a path 600 feet above the cloud top because it remembers the 500-foot vertical rule. Can it use that path under the ordinary cloud-clearance limits?

choices.A: No. The vertical minimum is 500 feet below a cloud, and the route directly above it does not meet the separate horizontal distance requirement.
choices.B: Yes. The same 500-foot minimum applies above or below any cloud.
choices.C: Yes. A drone above a cloud can ignore horizontal separation if flight visibility is at least three miles.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Section 107.51 specifies 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally. It does not supply a 500-foot above-cloud clearance option for a crossing directly over the cloud.
Why B is incorrect: The rule specifies below, rather than 500 feet in either direction.
Why C is incorrect: Meeting visibility does not remove the cloud-separation limits.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.51 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.51

questions.prompt: A paid drone delivery of a customer's package takes off and lands in State A. To avoid an obstacle it briefly flies across the state line into State B and returns before landing. Does the route satisfy the ordinary Part 107 intrastate condition on these facts?

choices.A: No. The operation does not remain wholly within the same state, even though both endpoints are in State A.
choices.B: Yes. A short detour can be disregarded if the package is not delivered in State B.
choices.C: Yes. Only the takeoff and landing states matter under the ordinary intrastate condition.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The condition concerns the whole operation rather than just its endpoints. The flight crosses into a second state.
Why B is incorrect: No brief-detour exception is provided by the rule described.
Why C is incorrect: Two endpoints in one state do not make the whole route intrastate.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.1 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.1
Reference: FAA, Part 107 package delivery FAQ — https://www.faa.gov/faq/package-delivery-allowed-under-small-uas-rule-part-107

questions.prompt: A pilot changes the flight app from miles per hour to knots. The team has a numeric speed gate on its checklist written in miles per hour. What should the team do before relying on that gate in flight?

choices.A: Confirm the units and convert or update the displayed gate consistently.
choices.B: Reuse the same numeric value because mph and knots are both measures of speed.
choices.C: Remove the gate because a digital app automatically enforces every operating limit.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: A speed number has meaning only with its unit. A consistent conversion preserves the intended gate.
Why B is incorrect: One knot is not one mile per hour.
Why C is incorrect: An app setting does not guarantee that the aircraft observes a crew-imposed limit.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A drone retailer flies a short outdoor demonstration to help sell a drone to a prospective customer. No separate fee is charged for the flight. Can the retailer use the limited recreational exception solely because the flight is free?

choices.A: Yes. A flight is recreational whenever the pilot charges no fee for that flight.
choices.B: No. The stated sales purpose is not strictly recreational.
choices.C: Yes. Sales demonstrations qualify as recreation if they last less than five minutes.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The purpose of the operation matters. A demonstration in support of a sale is not strictly recreational merely because there is no separate charge.
Why A is incorrect: Payment is not the only indicator of a nonrecreational purpose.
Why C is incorrect: The length of the flight does not change its sales purpose.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.1 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.1
Reference: FAA AIP, ENR 8.5, UAS Pilot Testing, Certification and Responsibilities — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aip_html/part2_enr_section_8.5.html
Reference: 49 U.S.C. § 44809, Exception for limited recreational operations of unmanned aircraft — https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/49/44809

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: On the first ground check, a warning occurs with Sensor A in Bay 1 and not Sensor B in Bay 2. After swapping detachable assemblies, the warning occurs in Bay 2 containing Sensor A.

Use the training troubleshooting record in the written scenario data. The technician exchanged two detachable position-sensor assemblies under the maintenance instructions. Which component should be investigated first based on where the warning moved?

choices.A: Bay 1's fixed wiring only.
choices.B: Sensor B.
choices.C: Sensor A.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: The warning appears at whichever bay contains Sensor A, so the fault follows that sensor assembly in this check.
Why A is incorrect: The warning moves away from Bay 1 after the exchange, so the evidence does not isolate that bay's fixed wiring.
Why B is incorrect: Sensor B shows no warning at either recorded bay.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.15 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.15
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A fixed-wing aircraft weighs 10.0 pounds. Its current CG is 4.2 inches aft of the datum. A 2.0-pound payload is moved 1.5 inches farther aft, with no other change. The aft CG limit is 4.4 inches. What is the result?

choices.A: The CG moves to 3.9 inches because an aft payload shift reduces the moment.
choices.B: The CG moves to 4.5 inches aft of the datum and exceeds the aft limit.
choices.C: The CG stays at 4.2 inches because the total weight is unchanged.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The move adds 3.0 pound-inches of moment. Dividing by 10.0 pounds gives a 0.3-inch aft shift, for a CG of 4.5 inches.
Why A is incorrect: Moving a payload farther aft increases the aft moment here.
Why C is incorrect: A weight can change the total moment by moving while total mass stays fixed.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 10, Weight and Balance — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 11, Aircraft Performance — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak

questions.prompt: A pilot builds a small drone solely for education and does not build it as a standard Remote ID aircraft. The drone is registered and will fly outside a FRIA. The pilot points to the home-built design exception in §89.501(c). What remains true?

choices.A: Recording the build date in a log automatically satisfies Part 89.
choices.B: The flight still needs an applicable operational Remote ID pathway or specific FAA authorization.
choices.C: The home-built production exception automatically permits flight without Remote ID anywhere.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The design and production exception does not erase the separate operational requirements for registered aircraft.
Why A is incorrect: A build log is not an operational compliance pathway.
Why C is incorrect: The exception concerns design and production. It is not a nationwide operating exception.
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.101 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.101
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.105 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.105
Reference: 14 CFR § 89.501 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-89/section-89.501

questions.prompt: An operator has a lawful unmanned aircraft operation under Part 91 and is transmitting ADS-B Out pursuant to §91.225. A colleague wants to apply the same Remote ID treatment to an ordinary Part 107 drone that merely carries an ADS-B receiver. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: Neither qualifies because §89.101 contains no Part 91 provision.
choices.B: Both operations qualify because receiving ADS-B is equivalent to transmitting ADS-B Out.
choices.C: The Part 89 Subpart B exception described applies to the qualifying Part 91 transmission. It does not extend to the Part 107 receiver-only operation.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 89.101(b) specifically excludes the stated Part 91 transmitting operation from Subpart B. A receiver on a Part 107 drone does not meet that condition.
Why A is incorrect: The rule explicitly recognizes qualifying Part 91 operations transmitting ADS-B Out.
Why B is incorrect: Reception and transmission are different functions. The operating framework also differs.

questions.prompt:
Written scenario data: Four-motor current readings in the stabilized hover test: the Center payload layout draws 12 A per motor. Each of the other equal-weight configurations exceeds 14 A on at least one motor. The continuous limit is 14 A per motor.

The written scenario data compares three payload arrangements of equal weight in a stabilized hover test. The operator's continuous limit is 14 A for each motor. Based on that criterion alone, which arrangement keeps every motor within the limit?

choices.A: Arrangement Left only.
choices.B: Arrangement Center only.
choices.C: Arrangement Forward only.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: The Center row shows 12 A on every motor. All four meet the 14 A per-motor limit.
Why A is incorrect: The Left row shows 15 A on M3, above the per-motor limit.
Why C is incorrect: The Forward row shows 16 A on M1, despite the lower readings elsewhere.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 11, Aircraft Performance — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 10, Weight and Balance — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A candidate Category 1 aircraft weighs exactly 0.55 pound with everything attached and will stay at that weight. It has no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate human skin on impact. For a proposed flight over people that does not involve an open-air assembly, what does the weight alone establish?

choices.A: The weight can qualify only if the attached equipment is removed during flight.
choices.B: The weight fails because Category 1 requires strictly less than 0.55 pound.
choices.C: The weight qualifies because the limit includes exactly 0.55 pound.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Section 107.110(a)(1) allows 0.55 pound or less on takeoff and throughout the operation.
Why A is incorrect: The stated total already includes attached equipment and does not exceed the limit.
Why B is incorrect: The cutoff is inclusive.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.110 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.110

questions.prompt: The planned launch is outside a thunderstorm's visible rain shaft, but beneath its spreading anvil. Lightning is seen between the storm and the work area. The crew expects no rain at the pad. What is the sound weather decision?

choices.A: Launch because lightning is confined to the visible shaft of heavy rain.
choices.B: Delay or relocate after reassessing the thunderstorm hazard, including lightning beyond the rain shaft.
choices.C: Launch if the drone can finish before the first raindrop reaches the pad.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Lightning can extend away from heavy rain. The visible activity near the planned route matters even if the pad stays dry.
Why A is incorrect: The edge of heavy rain does not bound the lightning hazard.
Why C is incorrect: Rain timing is not a safe substitute for evaluating the thunderstorm and its lightning.
Reference: FAA-H-8083-28B, Aviation Weather Handbook — https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A county owns a small unmanned aircraft that is not registered abroad. The county's survey unit is preparing its aircraft paperwork. Does Part 48 recognize this kind of public owner for registration eligibility?

choices.A: No. Local government aircraft can be registered only in a county vehicle system.
choices.B: No. Only aircraft held by individuals can be registered under Part 48.
choices.C: Yes. An aircraft of a political subdivision of a state can qualify.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: The eligibility rule includes aircraft of a state's political subdivision, such as a county.
Why A is incorrect: A local inventory system is not the same as FAA registration.
Why B is incorrect: The regulation includes public owners as well as eligible individuals.
Reference: 14 CFR § 48.20 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-48/section-48.20
Reference: 14 CFR § 48.25 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-48/section-48.25

questions.prompt: A remote PIC's Part 107 knowledge recency has lapsed. The pilot also holds a Part 61 private pilot certificate but is out of date on the Part 61 flight review. Which action can restore Part 107 knowledge recency without first completing the flight review?

choices.A: Complete FAA recurrent training available to remote pilots without a current Part 61 flight review.
choices.B: Renew the drone's aircraft registration.
choices.C: Take the training option that requires a current Part 61 flight review and disregard that prerequisite.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The general recurrent-training route under §107.65(b) does not require a current Part 61 flight review.
Why B is incorrect: Aircraft registration does not restore the pilot's aeronautical knowledge recency.
Why C is incorrect: The separate Part 61-based route requires the applicable flight review.
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.65 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.65
Reference: FAA, Become a Certificated Remote Pilot — https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/become_a_drone_pilot

questions.prompt: During a radio exercise, a controller requests an action. The trainee needs a standard response meaning the message is understood and the trainee will comply. Which term has that meaning?

choices.A: Say again.
choices.B: Wilco.
choices.C: Stand by.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Wilco combines understanding the message with an intention to comply.
Why A is incorrect: Say again requests repetition.
Why C is incorrect: Stand by asks the other station to wait.
Reference: FAA Pilot/Controller Glossary, Wilco and Mayday — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/pcg_html/
Reference: FAA AIM, §4-2, Radio Communications Phraseology and Techniques — https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap4_section_2.html

questions.prompt: A sea breeze meets an opposing low-level wind inland. The air converges along a narrow line, and clouds are growing along it. What motion best explains why the cloud line is forming?

choices.A: The meeting winds prevent any vertical motion, so the clouds must be unrelated.
choices.B: Air rises along the convergence line, cools, and can reach saturation.
choices.C: Air necessarily sinks along the convergence line and becomes more humid because it warms.

questions.explanation:
Why B works: Low-level convergence can force air upward. Rising air cools and can condense if it reaches saturation.
Why A is incorrect: Converging low-level flows can produce vertical motion.
Why C is incorrect: Sinking air generally warms, and the described cloud growth is consistent with lift.
Reference: FAA-H-8083-28B, Aviation Weather Handbook — https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook

questions.prompt: A proposed waiver covers the right-of-way requirement in §107.37(a) for a tightly coordinated demonstration. The operator wants the same waiver to allow operation close enough to another aircraft to create a collision hazard. Which part of §107.37 remains outside the waiver list?

choices.A: The prohibition in §107.37(b) against operating so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.
choices.B: Neither part, because relief from subsection (a) automatically covers subsection (b).
choices.C: The yielding requirement in §107.37(a), because only subsection (b) is waivable.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: Section 107.205 lists §107.37(a). It does not list §107.37(b), which separately prohibits creating a collision hazard.
Why B is incorrect: Relief from one subsection does not extend to another subsection.
Why C is incorrect: The list names (a), rather than (b).
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.37 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.37
Reference: 14 CFR § 107.205 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/section-107.205

questions.prompt: A level launch pad sits at the mouth of a narrow passage between two buildings. A ribbon shows much stronger and more irregular wind there than at an exposed alternate pad. The alternate provides good sight lines and the needed site access. Which plan is sound?

choices.A: Use the passage if the airport weather report lists a lower speed than the ribbon suggests.
choices.B: Use the narrow passage because wind always weakens between buildings.
choices.C: Evaluate and use the alternate if its actual conditions are within the aircraft and crew limits.

questions.explanation:
Why C works: Wind around buildings can be accelerated and turbulent in a passage. The alternate can reduce exposure if its conditions meet the limits.
Why A is incorrect: An airport observation does not override conditions at the actual launch site.
Why B is incorrect: Buildings do not guarantee shelter in a narrow gap.
Reference: FAA-H-8083-28B, Aviation Weather Handbook — https://www.faa.gov/regulationspolicies/handbooksmanuals/aviation/faa-h-8083-28b-aviation-weather-handbook
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf

questions.prompt: A visual observer has been scanning into bright glare for a long period. The crew brief allows a trained relief observer at a better viewing position. The operation can pause without increasing risk. What is the safest handover plan?

choices.A: Pause the task, brief and coordinate the replacement, and resume once required coverage is established.
choices.B: Swap the observers silently while the aircraft continues the critical maneuver.
choices.C: Tell the current observer to close both eyes briefly while the aircraft keeps flying the programmed path.

questions.explanation:
Why A works: The planned pause gives the crew time to transfer duties and verify coverage before resuming.
Why B is incorrect: A silent change can leave the pilot unaware that coverage has shifted or lapsed.
Why C is incorrect: A programmed path does not replace needed observation or coordination.
Reference: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, chs. 2 and 17, Decision-Making and Aeromedical Factors — https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak
Reference: FAA AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft System — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_107-2A.pdf
